about: Anomaly themes across coding rounds. Written by serendipity_harness.anomaly_log; decisions are made with its `set` command, not by editing this file.

themes.name: Information found by chance
themes.what: The founder comes across an article, a website or a technique while doing something else, and it sparks the idea.

history.note: Meets the three rules: one clear idea; bears on the research question; no trigger names information found by chance. Drafted code trigger-20, 6 papers.

themes.name: External shock or platform change
themes.what: Something outside the venture changes suddenly: a recession, a platform's policy or algorithm, a supplier ending a tool.

history.note: Split from outside timing (its technology-change half) and merged with external shock, once the study covered setbacks: both are outside changes in technology, rules or platforms.

themes.name: Idea from the founder's own experience
themes.what: The idea comes from the founder's own errand, thought or idle play, with no outside input.

searches.where: litreview full text + Paper list abstracts (base, FT50, R&T)
searches.query: user entrepreneurship; user entrepreneurs; personal frustration as source of idea
searches.note: Shah and Tripsas 2007 state it: users 'experienced a need in their day-to-day lives, created a solution' and became accidental entrepreneurs. No drafted trigger names it; Shah 2007 already supports background-02, background-11 and role-02.

themes.name: Unsought publicity from a third party or platform
themes.what: A YouTuber, an influencer or a platform (App Store, Shopify) promotes the product on its own initiative, with no request or offer to the founder.

history.note: Meets the three rules: one clear idea; bears on the research question; 2.5 is an offer made to the founder, while promotion is aimed at someone else's audience. Inductive: no paper read states it as a trigger. Two of four cases are clean; to be judged mainly on round 2.

themes.name: Outside timing or circumstance
themes.what: A wider change or a life event makes the moment right: maturing technology, a market turning to the founder's skills, a hurricane cleanup, a layoff.

history.note: Split from outside timing (its technology-change half) and merged with external shock, once the study covered setbacks: both are outside changes in technology, rules or platforms.

themes.name: Resources, contacts or knowledge as the result
themes.what: What comes of it is a supplier, a network of contacts, customer insights or new connections, not a product, market or growth.

history.note: Meets the three rules: one clear idea; bears on the research question; the outcome codes name a product, a market, growth or nothing. One code from drafted codes outcome-13, outcome-14 and outcome-17.

themes.name: Harmful result
themes.what: The event costs the venture: a lost channel, half of income gone, survival threatened.

history.note: Meets the three rules: one clear idea; bears on the research question; the study covers bad surprises; no outcome code names harm. Drafted code outcome-30.

themes.name: Outsider or naive start
themes.what: Not knowing an industry is told as an advantage: never having worked in a law firm, naivety as a superpower.

themes.name: The opportunity found them
themes.what: The founder tells the start as the opportunity finding them, without using luck words.

themes.name: Effort-only account
themes.what: The founder credits results wholly to work put in, with no role for chance.

searches.where: litreview full text + Paper list abstracts (base, FT50, R&T)
searches.query: attribution luck; self-serving attribution; entrepreneurs attribute success to effort not luck
searches.note: Brownell et al. 2024, p. 1698: entrepreneurs ranged from 'it's not luck at all' to luck as the majority. Drafted code rival-16 'Effort and persistence over luck' (daniels2019, merton2004, rosenman1988) states the theme.

themes.name: Breakthroughs noticed by founders close to customers
themes.what: A general theory from the founder: things start working through unplanned shifts that only founders close to customers notice.

themes.name: Limiting exposure to chance
themes.what: The founder deliberately screens out incoming opportunities to stay focused.

themes.name: A mission that draws people
themes.what: A nonprofit status and a resonant vision draw volunteers and trust.

themes.name: Find improved the product
themes.what: A chance find fixed the product's core design after founding, without growth or a change of direction.

themes.name: Change in technology, rules or platforms
themes.what: A change outside the founder's control in technology, rules or a platform the venture depends on opens a door or causes a setback: AI maturing, an iOS or search-engine update, a supplier dropping a tool.

history.note: Meets the three rules: one clear idea; bears on the research question; no trigger names a change in the world outside the founder. Drafted code trigger-12, widened to setbacks and platforms.

themes.why: Split from outside timing (its technology-change half) and merged with external shock, once the study covered setbacks: both are outside changes in technology, rules or platforms.

themes.name: Outside crisis or disaster
themes.what: A sudden, large outside event, such as a recession or a hurricane, opens an opportunity or threatens the venture.

history.note: Meets the three rules: one clear idea; bears on the research question; the study covers bad surprises. Drafted code trigger-11. Two cases.

themes.why: Split from outside timing (the hurricane) and external shock (the recession): sudden, large events rather than changes in technology or rules.
themes.note: Meets the three rules: one clear idea; bears on the research question; the study covers bad surprises. Drafted code trigger-11. Two cases.

themes.name: Personal misfortune
themes.what: A setback in the founder's own life, such as losing a job, sets off the venture.
themes.why: Split from outside timing: a personal event, not a change in the world.

searches.where: litreview full text + Paper list abstracts (base, FT50, R&T)
searches.query: job loss; unemployment entrepreneurship; necessity entrepreneurship
searches.note: Necessity-entrepreneurship papers found but not yet read. Drafted code trigger-10 'Personal misfortune turned into a venture' (busch2023, harmeling2013, sarasvathy2001) states the theme.

themes.name: Setback retold as a turning point
themes.what: The founder retells a setback, such as a layoff, a lost client, a failure or a slow start, as the moment that made the business.

anomalies.story: first client from failed business skills

searches.where: litreview full text + Paper list abstracts (base, FT50, R&T)
searches.query: blessing in disguise; turning point; reframed failure
searches.note: No new paper found. Brownell et al. 2024, p. 1711: a venture that capitalises on an event first seen as bad luck 'might later reframe that event as good luck'. Drafted code account-19 states the theme (brownell2024, garud2018, ma2002, sotosimeone2021).

searches.where: litreview full text (p-769c654c0b76)
searches.query: Coad and Storey 2021, cited by Soto-Simeone et al. 2021
searches.note: Read in full. p. 545: failed entrepreneurs 'frequently repackage their misfortunes as a learning opportunity, even if they didn't learn anything' (citing Ries 2011); also 'victory in the jaws of defeat'. A claim about failed founders' self-reports, not tested in the paper. Supports the self-serving side; Soto-Simeone et al. 2021 give the reappraisal side.

themes.name: The venture threatened or reshaped
themes.what: The event neither started, redirected nor advanced the venture: it threatened its survival, changed who ran it or changed how the founder works.

themes.name: Unbidden attention at the edge of 2.10
themes.what: Others' attention came unasked but outside the wording of 2.10: peers noticing results, influencers joining the founder's own affiliate programme, a search engine ranking the founder's post.

searches.where: litreview full text + Paper list abstracts (base, FT50, R&T)
searches.query: media coverage; word of mouth; publicity; influencer endorsement
searches.note: No held paper describes unsought promotion as a trigger. Leads to read: Teixeira and Brown 2018 (first customers of Airbnb, Etsy, Uber). Copeland 2023 has it only as an outcome (outcome-28). trigger-28 stays inductive.

themes.name: Legal claim from a third party
themes.what: An outsider's lawsuit or legal action forces a change.

themes.name: Sudden free time
themes.what: A cancelled job or a lost job leaves the founder with time that lets the idea surface or be worked on.

anomalies.story: the cancelled job and the pallets

themes.name: Setback from a supplier or the founder's own choice
themes.what: An operational setback: a carrier's delay, or a cost-saving choice that backfires.

themes.name: Another person's decision changes the founder's situation
themes.what: Someone else's decision, such as a boss starting a new venture or a teacher's instruction, changes the founder's situation and sets the story off.

themes.name: Disaster as the setting for a chance
themes.what: A disaster put the founder where a chance encounter happened; coded as a condition, not as the trigger 2.7.

themes.name: A customer's misfortune scatters contacts
themes.what: A client firm's near collapse moved known contacts into new firms, which became customers.

themes.name: Change in a market outside the venture
themes.what: An outside supply event, such as a famous mine closing, shifts demand.

themes.name: Adversity as a push
themes.what: Losing a customer pushed the founder to look again at suppliers and buyers.

themes.name: Lessons from past failures
themes.what: Past failures taught the founder to launch fast and test.

themes.name: Competing life commitments
themes.what: Another commitment, such as waiting for a military call-up, made the founder neglect the venture.

themes.name: A skill that built the audience
themes.what: A skill of the founder's built the following that later drew requests.

themes.name: Founding to learn
themes.what: The venture was started mainly as a way to learn, not to build a business.

themes.name: Founding told second-hand
themes.what: The founding is told by someone who did not live it, which bears on how far its surprise and search state can be trusted.

themes.name: Self-critical account of pivots
themes.what: The founder credits pivots with building the business but warns others against pivoting.

themes.name: A name or identity as the result
themes.what: What came of it was the business's name or identity.

themes.name: Goodwill as the result
themes.what: What came of it was an audience's goodwill and engagement.

themes.name: Demand that overwhelms
themes.what: A sudden rush of demand overloaded the operation, with no stated gain or loss.
